item.title: Samsung to use TSMC technology for Nvidia's next-generation memory chips, Seoul newspaper reports
item.description: Samsung Electronics will use TSMC's 3-nanometre process to produce base dies for Nvidia's next-generation custom high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) will use TSMC's (2330.TW) 3-nanometre process to produce base dies for Nvidia's (NVDA.O) next-generation custom high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on Sunday. The move would mark the first time Samsung has worked with the Taiwanese contract chipmaker at the HBM manufacturing stage, according to the report. Nvidia has asked Samsung, SK Hynix (000660.KS) and Micron Technology (MU.O) to use TSMC's process for NVHBM base dies, and sixth-generation DRAM technology for its core dies, the newspaper said, citing industry sources. NVHBM, unveiled in August, integrates Nvidia's custom memory controller into the base die and is aimed at standardising implementation across multiple memory suppliers, according to the company. Samsung accepted Nvidia's requirements after an internal review but plans to retain its in-house production model for standard HBM and custom products for other customers, Seoul Economic Daily said. It is also assessing whether its own foundry could produce NVHBM base dies if demand exceeds TSMC's capacity, the newspaper quoted an unnamed source as saying.

item.title: Turkey will get some diesel from US-Russia supply deal, energy minister says
item.description: Turkey will take some of the diesel Russia is supplying to global markets under its agreement with US President Donald Trump, Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Turkey will take some of the diesel Russia is supplying to global markets under its agreement with US President Donald Trump, Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said on Sunday. Bayraktar said the US-Russia [USN:L8N4610WB TEXT:"diesel supply deal"] was important in terms of energy security for Turkey. Ankara relies on Russia for some of its energy needs, as well as on Iran, Azerbaijan and others. It is trying to diversify through deals with the US and other partners. "Russia imposed restrictions on diesel exports in recent months when they started experiencing this problem. Now they reached a diesel deal with Trump... Through the talks we held, we will take some of that diesel to Turkey," Bayraktar told broadcaster Kanal 7. He did not elaborate. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European officials and some of Trump's fellow [USN:L1N45Z0VJ TEXT:"Republican politicians"] strongly criticised the deal. Bayraktar also said that Turkey plans to bring a second floating gas production platform online in the first quarter of 2028, adding that the platform would bring Turkey's daily output in the Black Sea to 45 million cubic metres. On Saturday, Turkey sent its [USN:L8N4611PM TEXT:"first floating gas production platform"], the Osman Gazi, to the Black Sea, a move Bayraktar has said is expected to roughly double daily output from its largest domestic gas field, the Sakarya field, to 20 million cubic metres from the current 9.5 million, equivalent to 7.3 billion cubic metres (bcm) annually. "In the first quarter of 2028, the second floating production platform is coming to Turkey and we will carry out 25 million cubic metres of production with it. It has a slightly bigger capacity (than Osman Gazi)," he said. "Therefore, with 45 million cubic metres, we will be using our own gas in three out of four homes in Turkey." He added that Turkey's daily production at the field would increase to 550,000 barrels of oil equivalent with the second floating platform. Turkey is one of Europe's largest gas markets, consuming 59 bcm last year. The country relies on imports for almost all its gas needs, with domestic production totalling 3.1 bcm last year, most of it from the Sakarya field. Bayraktar also said [USN:A4N3DZ01O TEXT:"hydrocarbon exploration operations"] planned off Pakistan had been delayed by about six months due to the Iran war's impact on the region.

item.title: In France's Limoges, the fire-ravaged town hall rekindles memories of Notre Dame
item.description: The 19th-century neo-Renaissance building survived two world wars.
item.dc:creator: Clotaire Achi
item.content:encoded: Residents in Limoges recoiled in horror on Sunday at the city's fire-ravaged town hall, an ornate 19th century neo-Renaissance building which survived two world wars but was torched by a masked mob during the [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"worst unrest"] to convulse France in years. Stunned onlookers had watched helplessly the previous evening as the blaze tore through the roof, felling the building's clock tower in scenes that revived haunting memories of the collapse of Notre Dame cathedral's spire in a 2019 fire. "It broke my heart. I saw Notre Dame all over again, except this time it was our town," said Francoise Faurie who witnessed the fire consume Limoges' town hall. Faurie's family had been due to celebrate her grand-daughter's baptism in the town hall in a month's time. "What kind of country are we living in? What are we leaving our children?" she said. "There's no reason to touch that building. You can have demands, you have the right to protest, but not the right to violence." EXTENSIVE DAMAGE The local prefect, Maurice Barate, said the roof had caved in onto lower floors, sparing only the west wing, and that large parts of the exterior had been destroyed. The destruction of the building, a listed monument that opened in 1883 and was inspired by Paris' city hall, was a "heritage catastrophe", he said. Its central clock tower and belfry towered 43 metres (141 feet) over the square below. "It's inadmissible to have burned down the town hall!" one local resident, Gilbert, said. "Those who did this need to be punished. They need to pay out of their own pocket, it's not for the state to pay." The town's shaken mayor, Guillaume Guerin, described how the local police force had quickly been overwhelmed by several hundred-strong mob who he said smashed windows and used a battering ram to break down the main door. "The logistics, the organisation, the premeditation behind yesterday’s attack on the town hall is something I find unbearable," he told reporters. Guerin said there had been insufficient police numbers to protect the building since officers from the national force had been deployed to the street protest. "I had no single national police officer to protect the town hall," the centre-right mayor continued. "This country is doing badly, this country is doing very badly, and it’s a small provincial mayor telling you so." Crowds gathered under blue skies as specialists surveyed the damage. Edith Lorcen, a retired nurse, expressed her shock at the malice of those behind the attack. "I'm disgusted. I'm hurting," Lorcen said. "But it does nothing to add hate on top of hate."

item.title: Davidovich Fokina overcomes Jodar to claim Shanghai crown
item.description: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina ended Rafael Jodar's dream run at the Shanghai Masters on Sunday, battling back to beat his fellow Spaniard 1-6 7-6(5) 6-4 and clinch the biggest title of his career.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina ended Rafael Jodar's dream run at the Shanghai Masters on Sunday, battling back to beat his fellow Spaniard 1-6 7-6(5) 6-4 and clinch the biggest title of his career. The 25th-seeded Davidovich Fokina is set to climb 13 places to a career-high world number 13 when the rankings are released on Monday. Jodar, playing in his first Masters 1000 final and the youngest Shanghai finalist in tournament history, made a blistering start, broke for a 2-0 lead and again to take the opening set. Davidovich Fokina recovered from a break down in the second set and saved break points in three successive service games before edging a tight tiebreak to force a decider. The momentum swung decisively in Davidovich Fokina's favour when he broke the 12th-seeded Jodar twice and sealed victory in two hours and 27 minutes. "I have a blank mind," Davidovich Fokina said. "I don't know what to say and I don't know how I feel. Just a huge relief. "After the first set I had to keep trying, keep pushing. In the tiebreak, I believed in myself again. In the third set, maybe I had a bit more fitness physically." It the third ATP singles title of the 27-year-old's career, adding to his ATP 250 triumphs in Chengdu and Mallorca this season. The first meeting between the two Spaniards pitted one of the ATP Tour's rising talents against a player enjoying the best season of his career. The 20-year-old Jodar, who was ranked outside the world's top 900 little more than a year ago, strengthened his bid to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin in his first full season on tour.

item.title: India widens cancer drug price caps, lowering prices of 137 medicines
item.description: India will reduce the prices of as many as 137 cancer drugs by 70%, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers said on Saturday, as it widened price controls in a bid to make treatment more affordable.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: India will reduce the prices of as many as 137 cancer drugs by 70%, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers said on Saturday, as it widened price controls in a bid to make treatment more affordable. Trade margins on the drugs will be limited to 30% of the maximum retail price, the ministry added. The medicines, which include immunotherapy drugs used for treating over 20 types of cancer, as well as for breast, prostate, colon, ovarian and cervical cancer, will be subject to the price changes from November 9. The latest decision builds on price controls introduced in 2019 on 42 anti-cancer drugs that cut prices by as much as 90%.

item.title: Albanian PM says mass protests a threat to EU membership, not government
item.description: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Sunday rejected calls to step down from growing street protests, and said they were a threat not to his government but to Albania's progress toward joining the European Union.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Sunday rejected calls to step down from growing street protests, and said they were a threat not to his government but to Albania's progress toward joining the European Union. Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities in the past week. Demonstrators demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings as well as banks and pulled up paving stones to throw at police, who have responded with tear gas, water cannon and [USN:L6N46303U TEXT:"rubber bullets."] The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful protests in the summer [USN:L6N42J18T TEXT:"against a luxury coastal development"] backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, pose the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and last year won a fourth term in office. "I am not being challenged, the government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged," Rama said in a live address on Facebook. “Albanians need to think very clearly: Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?” As Rama spoke, excavators were digging up and removing the paving outside his office in central Tirana as a new round of protests was expected. Corruption scandals have tarnished Albania's image over the years and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking. However, Rama has said his government is tackling corruption as never before. Along with Montenegro, Albania is currently leading the posse of Balkan countries seeking to join the EU, and is aiming for entry by 2030. Rama blamed unspecified foreign interests for the protests and for what he said was an attempted drone attack at his office this week. "God knows what the consequences will be. There are no young people, no students, and no minors who would even think of implementing this plan. This is a foreign hand," he said. Police said 388 people had been charged with criminal offences during the demonstrations. Scores of police officers and protesters have been injured.

item.title: Première apparition publique du pape depuis son opération pour un cancer du poumon
item.description: Le pape Léon XIV a promis dimanche de reprendre progressivement ses fonctions à la tête de l'Eglise catholique lors de sa première apparition publique depuis son opération subie il y a cinq jours pour un cancer du poumon.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le pape Léon XIV a promis dimanche de reprendre progressivement ses fonctions à la tête de l'Eglise catholique lors de sa première apparition publique depuis son opération subie il y a cinq jours pour un cancer du poumon. "Après avoir surmonté cette phase délicate (...), je vais maintenant reprendre peu à peu mes activités, toujours avec l'aide de Dieu et grâce à vos prières", a déclaré le souverain pontife, s'adressant d'une voix ferme et claire, depuis une fenêtre du palais apostolique du Vatican, à des milliers de fidèles rassemblés place Saint-Pierre. Agé de 71 ans, Léon XIV a subi mardi une opération visant à lui retirer le lobe inférieur du poumon droit après détection d'une tumeur maligne. Ce diagnostic, pour un pape connu pour être relativement jeune et énergique et qui n'a été élu qu'en mai 2025, a soulevé des questions quant à l'avenir de son pontificat alors qu'il doit faire face à la maladie.

item.title: EU condemns attacks by violent settlers, including on diplomats, spokesperson says
item.description: The European Union "strongly condemns" attacks by violent settlers in the West Bank, including against European diplomats, the bloc's foreign policy spokesperson said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The European Union "strongly condemns" attacks by violent settlers in the West Bank, including against European diplomats, the bloc's foreign policy spokesperson said on Sunday. The statement came a day after Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian civilians, European diplomats and a French mayor in the occupied West Bank. "We take positive note of statements by several Israeli representatives who condemned the attacks but we expect full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists," the EU spokesperson said.

item.title: One killed, 15 injured in Ukrainian drone attack on St Petersburg and Leningrad region
item.description: Ukrainian drones struck oil facilities and logistics and data centers, local authorities said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: One person was killed and 15 were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on oil facilities, logistics and data centres in Russia's St Petersburg and the Leningrad region, local authorities said on Sunday. St Petersburg's governor Alexander Beglov said fires had broken out at the St Petersburg oil terminal, an oil depot and industrial warehouses. Russian e-commerce company Ozon said that its logistics hub in St Petersburg was on fire and the internet company VK (VKCO.MM) said that its data centre in the Leningrad region had been attacked by drones, but services were available to users as normal. Ukrainian drone producer Fire Point said on Sunday that the Ukrainian military had struck a VK data centre near St Petersburg. Russian air defence units downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Russian Defence Ministry said. Russia is constantly responding to Ukrainian attacks with systematic, large-scale strikes, the TASS news agency reported on Sunday, citing Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. "The Kyiv regime is resisting. But this cannot change the course of events," he said, answering a question about how Russia might respond to Kyiv's attack on St Petersburg.

item.title: IMF/World Bank meetings leave developing countries with more questions than answers
item.description: Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Shalal, David Lawder
item.content:encoded: Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble. Not for the first time, [USN:L1N46302K TEXT:"lower-income countries"] are being rocked by the spillover from the actions of wealthier nations: rising debt service costs, higher inflation and the risk of falling ever further behind economically thanks to the AI boom. What they got was the stock advice the global lenders always dish out: to shrink fiscal deficits and accelerate economic reforms to attract more private sector investment. Kristalina Georgieva, the first IMF chief from a developing nation - Bulgaria - said advanced economies were in fact the worst offenders on budget imbalances. She noted that developing countries' debt levels had actually fallen in recent years, only for surging bond yields elsewhere to drive up their borrowing costs. Average debt service payments there had more than doubled from a decade ago to 14% of government revenue, crowding out education, healthcare and other critical areas, she said. ADVANCED ECONOMIES FOCUSED ON THEIR OWN PROBLEMS At a panel on Saturday, Georgieva said many issues remained unresolved, especially around AI: "We are in a place where we have many more questions than we have answers. And my alert to everybody is: Do not fall for the guys that pretend they have the answers. They are tricking you." Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council think tank, said the meetings had flunked their opportunity to come up with guidance or ways to help. "It's hard to talk about the developing world when the advanced economies don't have their act together and are at risk of a fiscal crisis," he said. "And that's on top of political situations in many of these countries that makes development aid not a priority at the moment." Mauricio Cardenas, Colombia's former finance minister and now a research scholar at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs in New York, said many policymakers were left with a deep sense that "something really bad could happen" but no real roadmap to navigate the future. "The IMF and World Bank are not particularly well prepared for this new phase. They understand that something is going on, they bring in experts on AI," he said. "But in the end, there's no kind of specific, concrete advice on how to be prepared for something where you don't really understand how it's going to unfold." The geopolitical tensions that have roiled both institutions since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - complicating concerted action - were also evident in Bangkok when nearly half the delegates at an [USN:L1N46301V TEXT:"IMF steering committee"] walked out when Russia's finance minister spoke. Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport delayed the arrival of the head of that committee, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who had to travel overland to Qatar to catch a flight. And Bangkok itself was a stark reminder of the challenges facing developing countries, still partly under water after floods in September that caused almost $200 million in damage to Thailand's industrial sector. RISING INEQUALITY COULD RAISE COSTS IN LONG TERM Kate Pickett, a professor at the University of York, urged policymakers to focus on more inclusive growth rather than forcing developing countries into tough structural reforms. "If inequality increases, if poverty deepens, that will increase their costs in the long term," she said. "It's not enough to describe an economy as resilient. It's only resilient for the rich and the privileged.” Ayhan Kose, deputy chief economist at the World Bank, said the global economy had weathered its biggest energy shock - from the US-Israeli war on Iran - better than expected. But while a global recession had been avoided, he said growth outlooks in both developing and advanced economies were worse than before. Growth had already fallen off in half of advanced economies, while in developing countries as a whole, it had slowed significantly to around 3.6% from 4.4%. “People are really worried because resilience today is not a guarantee for resilience tomorrow," he said. "Now they are worried about what will be the next shock, because every six months, if not every three months, there is a new shock." While no specific initiatives were announced, he said the World Bank remained focused on helping developing countries prepare for advancements in AI, in part by mobilising more private capital, now at triple the levels of 2022. Yet it, too, has to contend with sharp drops in official development aid and persistent challenges in attracting foreign investment to developing countries. “The reality on the ground is the reality on the ground,” he said.

item.title: L'Egypte prête à contribuer à la sécurité de l'Arabie saoudite
item.description: L'Egypte est prête à apporter à l'Arabie saoudite le soutien nécessaire à la défense de sa sécurité et de sa stabilité face aux attaques des Houthis, a déclaré dimanche la présidence égyptienne.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Egypte est prête à apporter à l'Arabie saoudite le soutien nécessaire à la défense de sa sécurité et de sa stabilité face aux attaques des Houthis, a déclaré dimanche la présidence égyptienne. Le président égyptien Abdel Fattah al Sissi a demandé la tenue d'une session parlementaire dans la journée afin d'autoriser l'armée égyptienne, l'une des plus importantes et des plus puissantes de la région, à contribuer à la défense du royaume si celui-ci en faisait la demande. "L'Egypte apportera à l'Arabie saoudite toutes les formes de soutien nécessaires et possibles pour défendre sa sécurité et sa stabilité, protéger ses ressources, son intégrité territoriale et les lieux saints de l'islam", a déclaré la présidence égyptienne dans un communiqué. Ces derniers jours, les Houthis, soutenus par l'Iran, ont pris pour cible l'aéroport international de Ryad ou encore des installations de la compagnie publique pétrolière Aramco. L'Egypte et l'Arabie saoudite sont des partenaires stratégiques et économiques étroits. Ryad et d'autres pétromonarchies du Golfe ont fourni à l'Egypte des aides se montant à des milliards de dollars après le renversement par l'armée du président islamiste Mohamed Morsi en 2013.

VATICAN CITY, Oct 18 (Reuters) – Pope Leo spoke to crowds in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday in his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago, smiling from a window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice.

The 71-year-old pontiff had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fuelling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.

Leo came to the window in the palace unaided on Sunday and held his weekly noon-time appointment as usual. He thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would slowly return to full duty as leader of the 1.4-billion member Church.

Show Full Article

“Having overcome this delicate phase … I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers,” Leo said.

He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God “without compromise”.

(Reporting by Joshua McElwee;Editing by Sara Rossi and Helen Popper)

item.title: Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
item.description: Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday. Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an [USN:L1N42P0Q6 TEXT:"interim ceasefire"] collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response but [USN:L1N45X04L TEXT:"Iran’s security chief"] said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all [USN:L1N45Q01J TEXT:"seven conditions"] for reopening the strait. "Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Iran's conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, the lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts. If Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with talks resuming the following day, Araqchi said. A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's [USN:L1N45T0JD TEXT:"nuclear programme"] from the outset. US Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' eight-month war. Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway.

item.title: Accenture looks to sell Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, FT reports
item.description: IT consulting firm Accenture is looking to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: IT consulting firm Accenture (ACN.N) is looking to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Accenture has hired JPMorgan (JPM.N) to work on a strategic review of the China business after receiving unsolicited interest in the unit over the past year, the report added. Accenture and JPMorgan did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment outside regular business hours. The sale process is likely to draw interest from private equity groups and a small cluster of strategic buyers, the report said. Accenture may opt to retain a significant minority stake in the business, the report added. Accenture’s Greater China operations include Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China, according to its website. The consultancy firm recently forecast full-year 2027 revenue growth between 3% and 6%, above analysts' estimates.

item.title: Egypt says ready to give Saudi Arabia necessary support amid Houthi conflict
item.description: Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensify their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensify their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter. Egyptian President [USN:L8N46306J TEXT:"Abdel Fattah al-Sisi"] had requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the region's largest and most powerful, to help defend Saudi Arabia if the kingdom requested its support. The Houthis have in recent days attacked [USN:S8N44Y00K TEXT:"Riyadh's international airport"] and the state oil giant [USN:S8N44D022 TEXT:"Saudi Aramco"], amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce. "Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement. It followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief. Parliament was due to hold the urgent session at 1 p.m. (1000 GMT) to vote on authorising the request. Sisi said in a [USN:L8N46306J TEXT:"speech"] on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited. Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist President Mohamed Morsi in 2013. Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role.

item.title: Pope Leo pledges gradual return to duties in first event since cancer surgery
item.description: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago. The 71-year-old pontiff had an [USN:S8N42Y05U TEXT:"operation"] on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, [USN:L8N4600P9 TEXT:"fuelling speculation"] about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy. Smiling from a window of the Vatican's Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule. "Having overcome this delicate phase... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers," Leo said. The pope, who was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on Saturday, came to the window in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual. He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God "without compromise". NUN CRIES AS LEO MAKES APPEARANCE Leo has been diagnosed with [USN:L8N46006S TEXT:"lung adenocarcinoma"], the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades, who was elected only in May 2025, caused shock. His doctors discharged him on Saturday after blood tests and chest imaging that day showed him well enough to return home. They said he was able to perform normal daily activities independently. Crowds in St. Peter's Square, numbering about 15,000 according to the Vatican, shouted and clapped loudly as Leo first appeared at the window on Sunday. One Catholic nun knelt and cried, holding her hand over her face. A few steps away, a group of other nuns held aloft a sign reading, "Best wishes, Holy Father. We love you and we are praying for you". POPE'S CALENDAR IN FLUX Leo usually keeps a busy schedule, but the Vatican has cancelled his other public events until at least Wednesday, when he is due to hold a weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square. It has not said whether he will hold that audience. The pope is also planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader [USN:L8N45D0VL TEXT:"in decades"]. Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the pope's lead surgeon, said on Saturday that Leo could be fully recovered in time for that trip. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state, has however expressed scepticism. He told journalists on Friday the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward "according to the condition of his health".

item.title: Paris condamne l'agression d'un maire français par des colons juifs
item.description: La France a condamné dimanche l'agression "gravissime" par des colons juifs du maire d'Aulnoye-Aymeries survenue la veille dans le village palestinien de Taybeh.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La France a condamné dimanche [USN:L8N46309E TEXT:"l'agression"] "gravissime" par des colons juifs du maire d'Aulnoye-Aymeries survenue la veille dans le village palestinien de Taybeh. Dans un communiqué, le Quai d'Orsay a exprimé "son soutien et sa solidarité" à l'égard des représentants de plusieurs missions diplomatiques, dont le consul général de France à Jérusalem et ses homologues belge et polonais également pris à partie lors de cette attaque. "La France appelle les autorités israéliennes à arrêter les auteurs de cette agression gravissime et à les traduire en justice. Au-delà, les autorités israéliennes doivent prendre toutes les mesures nécessaires pour faire cesser ces actes de terreur", a souligné le ministère des Affaires étrangères. "La France réitère sa condamnation de la politique de colonisation. La colonisation est contraire au droit international. Elle porte une atteinte grave aux droits des Palestiniens, menace la stabilité de la Cisjordanie et compromet la solution à deux Etats", a-t-il ajouté.

item.title: Roy Cooper's North Carolina playbook is working. Can other Democrats copy it?
item.description: North Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly 20 years, but former Governor Roy Cooper, who hasn't lost an election in four decades, has built a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley.
item.dc:creator: Yasmeen Abutaleb
item.content:encoded: North Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in nearly 20 years, but former Governor Roy Cooper has built a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley by relentlessly focusing on affordability and a blunt promise to “make stuff cost less.” At campaign stops, Cooper, 69, points to his six-year fight to expand Medicaid through a Republican-controlled legislature as evidence he can work across party lines, while attacking Trump-backed healthcare cuts that he says are hitting North Carolinians hard. “People should not have to make a choice between going to a doctor and putting food on the table,” Cooper said at a September 26 rally in Raleigh, North Carolina. “This 'Big Beautiful Bill' that gave tax cuts to billionaires has now driven healthcare premiums up more than double for people.” The White House says the bill cuts taxes, protects Medicaid for eligible Americans and curbs fraud and abuse. Cooper's message appears to be working: His lead stood at 14 points in an October SurveyUSA poll. The top super PAC for Senate Republicans has paused TV advertising in North Carolina less than three weeks before the election and begun shifting campaign dollars to defend seats in states that include Iowa and Kansas. President Donald Trump will rally in the state on Tuesday for Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair who has never held elected office. The question for Democrats is whether Cooper's playbook can help them win Republican and independent voters elsewhere, or whether his success is unique to a popular former governor who has never lost an election in four decades of public service. While some Democrats in heavily Democratic states have embraced Medicare for All, which would provide government-run health insurance for all Americans, Cooper has focused on expanding existing coverage and lowering costs. He points to his fight to expand Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and campaigns on prescription drug and insurance costs. 'OUR STAR ATHLETE AND NO ONE'S PAYING ANY ATTENTION' “It’s like he’s our star athlete and no one’s paying any attention,” said Neera Tanden, president of the Center for American Progress, a Democratic-aligned think tank, and former White House adviser to President Joe Biden. “The strength of Roy Cooper’s campaign is that he’s able to attract Democrats and independents, but also even some Republicans because he’s focused on cost, but he also has a record.” Paul Shumaker, a longtime Republican strategist in North Carolina, attributes Cooper’s success to the fact he was already well-known and that Whatley failed to distinguish himself from Trump. “Roy Cooper came to the US Senate race with a known brand that has been trusted by a majority of North Carolina voters election after election,” Shumaker said. “Republicans are suffering from a lack of trust on the economy right now and Whatley has failed to reestablish that trust.” Cooper declined an interview request for this story. The Whatley campaign did not respond to a request for comment. WINNING OVER INDEPENDENTS North Carolina’s electorate is unusually independent: 40% of registered voters are unaffiliated with either party, compared with 30% each for Republicans and Democrats. Republicans, however, have dominated the state legislature for more than a decade and redrawn districts to strengthen their grip. Like other Republican candidates, Whatley must contend with Trump’s record-low approval rating, which now hovers at 32%, according to an October [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"Reuters/Ipsos poll"]. That poll also showed registered voters preferring Democrats over Republicans nationally by 44% to 37%. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, with 28% of independent voters still undecided. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the US Senate, where Democrats must net four seats in the November 3 midterm elections to control the chamber — an already difficult task that makes Cooper's North Carolina race especially important. Cooper's signature bipartisan achievement did not come easily. It took him six years to persuade the Republican-controlled state legislature to pass an expansion of Medicaid under Obamacare in 2023, extending health insurance to more than 700,000 state residents, according to state health department data. After passage, he called it “an unnecessarily long and agonizing journey.” Whit Ayres, a Republican pollster, said several moderate Democratic governors in the South could replicate Cooper’s success, including Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear. “The Roy Coopers of the world are not unique,” Ayres said. “The Republicans nominated someone who’s never been elected to any public office at any level anywhere running against a reasonably moderate, popular governor.” RUNNING AGAINST HEALTHCARE CUTS Many of the state’s Medicaid gains are likely to be undone by Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” a sweeping tax and budget bill the Republican-led Congress passed last year that cuts about $1 trillion from Medicaid, the largest cut in the program’s history, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. Cooper has used Trump’s signature domestic legislative achievement to paint the president and Republicans as depriving North Carolinians of healthcare in order to give billionaires more tax cuts. He has also focused on congressional Republicans’ decision to curtail COVID-era Obamacare subsidies last year, causing healthcare premiums on the individual health insurance marketplace to spike and more than 200,000 state residents to drop their coverage, according to health policy research firm KFF. “Roy Cooper has always polled over Republicans,” said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. “This will be the average election for Roy Cooper.”

item.title: Microsoft pulls out of UK data center deal with Nscale, Telegraph reports
item.description: Microsoft has pulled out of a data center deal with British cloud provider Nscale, Britain's Telegraph newspaper reported on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Microsoft (MSFT.O) has pulled out of a data center deal with British cloud provider Nscale, Britain's Telegraph newspaper reported on Sunday. The US tech giant, one of Nscale's two largest customers, recently terminated its agreement for the data center in Loughton, Essex, according to the report. The newspaper did not specify why Microsoft withdrew from the project, and Microsoft did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside regular business hours. The Telegraph report said Nscale had faced repeated delays with the project. National power grid officials, it reported, had told Nscale they did not expect a power supply for the data center until the 2030s. "Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," an Nscale spokesperson told Reuters. "We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK." Nscale filed for an [USN:L4N45A197 TEXT:"initial public offering"] in the US last month, with Microsoft and Anthropic expected to be its major customers, according to its prospectus. Nscale [USN:L4N45A1JP TEXT:"provides"] infrastructure, including compute, power and data centers, as well as software for training and running AI models. The Nvidia-backed (NVDA.O) AI group, which competes against CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , Nebius (NBIS.O) , Crusoe and Lambda, has grown rapidly since its launch, scaling from $100 million to more than $103 billion in total contracted value in just two-and-a-half years.

item.title: Carney’s pipeline push is unlikely to bring back Canada’s oil jobs boom
item.description: Even Mark Carney won’t call it a boom. While Canada’s oil output may rise, experts don’t expect to see major job creation.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson
item.content:encoded: A Syncrude oil sands plant outside the Alberta oil hub of Fort McMurray, seen from a helicopter. Alberta's oil sands contain one of the world's largest unconventional petroleum reserves in a thick, sticky form of oil called bitumen. Canada's Prime Minister, Mark Carney, wants to export more oil to Asia to blunt the impact of President Donald Trump's tariffs. REUTERS/Todd Korol Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney is betting a new pipeline can help revive the country’s oil industry, boost its production and exports, and reduce its dependence on the United States. Bringing back jobs will be much harder. In the Alberta oil hub of Fort McMurray – nicknamed Fort McMoney in its heyday more than a decade ago – the tens of thousands of oil field jobs that powered the last boom are unlikely to return, even if Carney gets his pipeline. Instead, much of the growth in oil sands output is likely to come from automation and efficiency gains rather than large-scale hiring, according to industry forecasts and nearly a dozen interviews with company officials, workers, politicians and academics. The pipeline backed by Carney would transport 1 million barrels of crude oil a day to a port on the Pacific coast, expanding export capacity to Asia. Asked by Reuters what the pipeline would mean for the region’s economy, Carney – a former central banker – cautioned against anticipating a return to the oil-boom days. "I wouldn't use the term 'boom'," Carney said during a visit to Fort McMurray this month. "I would use ‘sustained growth’." A giant dump truck hauls unprocessed oil at a Suncor mine near Fort McMurray, Alberta. REUTERS/Todd Korol A construction worker on the job at a new commercial building in the Alberta oil sands hub of Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol MORE OIL, FEWER WORKERS More oil without many more permanent jobs could leave Carney politically exposed on two fronts: Critics on the left say his efforts to fast-track the project’s regulatory approval risks sacrificing the environment, while those on the right argue the deregulation should deliver faster economic growth, higher salaries and more oil jobs. Low job growth could also further fuel Alberta’s separatist movement, though a referendum on whether to hold a vote to leave Canada is expected to fail on Monday. An August labor forecast by industry group Energy Safety Canada projects that oil sands employment will fall by 920 jobs or 4% by 2035, even as production grows 6%. A spokesperson for Energy Safety Canada told Reuters that a new West Coast pipeline would likely reverse the projected job decline but may not add many permanent jobs because of the “structural trend” of producing more oil with fewer workers. "Nobody should expect that something that happened 15 years ago will happen the same way today," said Dianna De Sousa, CEO of the Fort McMurray Chamber of Commerce. A spokesperson for Carney declined to comment on the lackluster projections for job creation from the pipeline, referring questions to the Department of Natural Resources, which did not respond. FROM BOOM TO BUST TO WILDFIRES From 2000 to 2014, Canadian and international oil companies spent billions to build out the mega-mines and other facilities required to extract bitumen, the thick oil found in northern Alberta. Fort McMurray became a place where workers fresh out of high school could earn six-figure salaries, putting new pickups and pricey boats in their driveways. A boarded-up hotel for sale offers a reminder of the downturn in Fort McMurray's fortunes. REUTERS/Todd Korol Colorful trees grow in a burnt-out forest outside Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol A new community of houses in Fort McMurray. Housing values have declined sharply over the last decade. REUTERS/Todd Korol Rush-hour traffic on a major downtown street in Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol A delivery driver walks to a store in downtown Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol Sarah Thapa, owner of Avenue Eatery and Cafe in Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol Guests look at a display in the local Oil Sands Museum. REUTERS/Todd Korol Fly-in, fly-out workers — some from as far as 5,000 km (3,107 miles) away – packed on-site work camps because the city lacked housing. Then came the 2015 oil price crash, followed by a devastating wildfire one year later. Investors’ growing focus on environmental, social and governance (ESG) criteria combined with the climate policies of Carney's predecessor Justin Trudeau deepened the slump. Nobody should expect that something that happened 15 years ago will happen the same way today. Dianna De Sousa, CEO of the Fort McMurray Chamber of Commerce International oil majors exited. Annual oil sands capital investment fell from a C35billion(24.55 billion) peak in 2014 to C$14.2 billion in 2024, according to Statistics Canada. The last major new oil sands project, Suncor's Fort Hills, started up in 2018. Alberta’s oil and gas sector employs 435,000 people today, including temporary and part-time workers, 85,000 fewer than in 2014, according to data from Alberta’s Servus Credit Union. Real disposable income in the province is still 10% below 2014 levels. Housing values have declined sharply. Stronger oil prices and rising production have brought some signs of recovery, including regional population growth for the first time in a decade. But flights from Calgary and other major cities sometimes arrive nearly empty, and vacant commercial spaces dot downtown. "Things are not getting better," said Jenny Parsons, who has worked as a truck driver and contractor at oil sands sites since moving from Newfoundland 15 years ago. She said she was earning barely a dollar more an hour than she was in 2011. Jenny Parsons says her wages have flatlined since the boom collapsed over a decade ago. She will vote yes on Monday to holding a referendum on Alberta separation. REUTERS/Todd Korol WHAT A PIPELINE COULD BRING No oil sands company has committed the C$100 billion in private investment needed to fill the proposed pipeline and build the carbon capture and storage project Carney has made a condition of federal approval. Kendall Dilling, head of the Oil Sands Alliance, which represents the five largest companies, said the projects could create thousands of jobs across Canada by the mid-2030s, including upstream investment and supply-chain activity as well as pipeline construction. But many of these jobs would be temporary construction jobs, in British Columbia as well as Alberta, rather than permanent oil-industry jobs. Some of those jobs no longer exist. Efficiency gains, for example, have cut the time oil companies spend on routine maintenance, which has reduced the number of staff as well as contract positions, he said. The employment gains “may be less than the absolute peaks that we've seen in the past.” Jason Kenney, Alberta's conservative premier from 2019 to 2022, cut corporate taxes to get oil sands companies to spend on big projects. But even after oil prices rose and revenue stabilized, companies prioritized shareholder returns over job growth, he told Reuters. "I was certainly frustrated with them,” he told Reuters. He said he urged companies to allocate some of the tax cut savings to their capital plans. "The people need to see a benefit, not just the shareholder in New York." A Suncor oil sands mine outside Fort McMurray. The company launched the last major new oil sands project in the area in 2018. REUTERS/Todd Korol The industry group representing oil companies did not respond directly to Kenney's comments but said the pipeline provided an opportunity to increase production, create jobs and grow government revenue. CARNEY FACES RISKS FROM LEFT AND RIGHT By backing a new pipeline, Carney — who grew up in Alberta's capital of Edmonton — has brokered an uneasy truce between the federal government and Alberta conservatives. But he has angered some in his own Liberal party by embracing oil to help the Canadian economy survive President Donald Trump’s tariffs. He has repealed many of Trudeau's environmental policies, cut the tax rate on new capital investment, and is promoting Canadian oil to investors abroad. While Carney’s approval rating was at 62% in a September poll from Angus Reid, public sentiment on energy and the environment can shift quickly. "It's important to remember that the environmental policies of Justin Trudeau were widely popular at the time," said Lori Williams, a political science professor at Calgary’s Mount Royal University. "If we see more environmentally friendly options starting to come on in the future then I think additional pipelines in Canada will be much harder to sell." Fort McMurray's boom had its downsides. The flood of workers strained local infrastructure and created tensions between locals and the thousands of people in work camps. Some oil sands companies now hire more locals to reduce their reliance on fly-in workers, a shift that reflects a leaner but steadier industry. Still, longtime residents like Colin Hartigan, owner of the city’s Coldwell Banker United office, hope that Carney's ambitions will bring back at least an echo of the old Fort McMurray. "At some point, there's going to be another boom," Hartigan said. "Do I think families here want to see that? Not like in the past, that was a little bit crazy. But do we all pray for it? Absolutely." The Suncor oil sands mine outside Fort McMurray. The company is one of the major producers in the oil patch. REUTERS/Todd Korol

item.title: France counts cost of worst unrest in years
item.description: One demonstrator died, hundreds of police were injured and nearly 1,800 people arrested while violent fringe groups targeted public buildings and looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets.
item.dc:creator: Sybille de La Hamaide
item.content:encoded: France woke on Sunday to the wreckage of one of its most violent days of unrest in years after protests over high prices and public services left one demonstrator dead, hundreds of police injured and nearly 1,800 people arrested. Nationwide demonstrations erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops ransacked, and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country. One protester died after suffering a cardiac arrest during [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"demonstrations"] in Paris, where police made a record 855 arrests. Across France, more than 500 officers were injured, the interior minister said. "It's like a war zone here," said Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who had come to Paris with his children to visit a friend and said the protests forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique, which suffered major damage on Saturday. More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities, marking the convergence of a month-long [USN:L6N45M1EJ TEXT:"student movement"] with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services. President Emmanuel Macron will address the nation at 2000 local time (1800 GMT) on Sunday, his office said. SEVERAL HUNDRED SHOPS DAMAGED While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers. A massive clean-up operation began in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said several hundred shops had been damaged on Saturday. In Paris, smashed shop windows, burnt-out bicycles and spray-painted slogans bore witness to a day that began largely with peaceful demonstrations but descended into violence. In [USN:L1N46402C TEXT:"Limoges"], southwestern France, mayor Guillaume Guerin denounced the chaos after the city's 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze and partially destroyed in an arson attack on Saturday, drawing comparisons to the 2019 fire that devastated Paris's Notre-Dame Cathedral. "There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives," Guerin told Reuters. He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the million euros needed to repair the city hall. The unrest has increased pressure on President Macron and his government, with a presidential election due next year. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals. Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. "Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos," Lescure said in a statement. Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 stores had been looted in his city, while Marseille Mayor Benoit Payan announced emergency financial aid to support those businesses impacted by the violence. French retailer Carrefour's <CARR.PA> Chief Executive Alexandre Bompard told BFMTV that 50 of the company's shops had been damaged including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into the dozens of millions of euros. The protests began last month over school conditions and teacher shortages in working-class suburbs, before broadening into a movement against inequality, public spending cuts and the rising cost of living.

item.title: Japan PM Takaichi's support rate falls below 50%, lowest since taking office, Kyodo reports
item.description: The approval rating for Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration fell below 50% to its lowest level since she took office in October last year, Kyodo News Agency reported on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The approval rating for Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration fell below 50% to its lowest level since she took office in October last year, Kyodo News Agency reported on Sunday. In a poll conducted between October 17 and 18, the approval rating for Takaichi's administration was 49.1%, the report said. The decline might have been affected by Takaichi's slow response surrounding the resignation of Kazuo Yana as the nation's farm minister, the report said. Yana [USN:L6N4600KT TEXT:"stepped down"] from the post on Wednesday after coming under fire for remarks about cutting road funding for municipalities that did not support him. Some 57.7% of respondents said Takaichi's decision to replace him came "too late," Kyodo said, while 81.5% said it was natural for Yana to resign. Takaichi appointed Yana in a cabinet reshuffle last month, but had openly chided him in parliament for the remarks over the road funding, which local media first reported earlier this month.

item.title: Australia's Smith says head blow left him anxious in first test concussion scare
item.description: Australia batsman Steve Smith said he was anxious after being hit on the head and facing the prospect of another concussion after a blow playing against South Africa in the first test a week ago.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australia batsman Steve Smith said he was anxious after being hit on the head and facing the prospect of another concussion after a blow playing against South Africa in the first test a week ago. Former captain Smith has previously suffered multiple concussions in his career, and he had to go through concussion protocols after a bouncer from Anrich Nortje hit him on the helmet last Monday during the second-last day of the clash at Kingsmead in Durban. “I was a little bit anxious after the hit, to be honest,” Smith said on Sunday before the start of the second test at St George’s Park in a television interview. “It was a decent knock, and the rest of that day, I wasn't travelling too well, and I think it was more to do with anxiety, of hoping not to feel what I felt in the past, waking up the next morning and things like that. “So, yeah, fortunately, I woke up well. I passed all the tests, and things recovered pretty quickly,” Smith added as he prepared to take part in the rain-delayed second test. The 37-year-old was assessed on the field by the physio and the doctor, and his helmet was changed as is mandatory for all such hits, but he continued his innings, scoring 27 runs as Australia built a large lead. PASSED CONCUSSION PROTOCOLS But then Smith did not take to the field at the start of South Africa's second innings on Monday, instead being subjected to the concussion protocols, which he passed. He returned from the start of the last day’s play on Tuesday to help his side to a 214-run victory and a 1-0 lead in the three-match series. Smith, who is 28 short of 11,000 test runs, was the first player replaced in a test after the introduction of a concussion substitute. He was struck on the back of the head by a Jofra Archer bouncer in the 2019 Ashes test at Lord's in London. He also suffered a concussion after being hit on the head in practice during Australia's One Day International series in England in 2020 and two months later, back home in Sydney, woke on the morning of the second ODI against India with vertigo and was sick. There have also been incidents in Sri Lanka in 2022, at the last World Cup in India and last December in the Ashes at Adelaide where he was ruled out of the third test about 20 minutes before the toss with a vestibular issue, the sensory system located in the inner ear that controls balance and spatial orientation.

item.title: Hurricanes riding high but not looking past league-worst Flames
item.description: The Carolina Hurricanes are riding a seven-game winning streak and sitting atop the Eastern Conference standings.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The Carolina Hurricanes are riding a seven-game winning streak and sitting atop the Eastern Conference standings. Even so, the defending Stanley Cup champions are not patting themselves on the back as they head to Calgary to face the struggling Flames. The Hurricanes extended their run with a 3-2 comeback victory over the Winnipeg Jets on Saturday to open a five-game road trip, but they admit it was far from their best. "We know we've got a lot better than we did (Saturday)," said forward Nikolaj Ehlers, whose power-play goal broke a 2-2 tie in the third period. "We're not exactly where we want to be, but it's a long season, and we've got a lot of time to keep making the small details better." The win may not have been a masterpiece, but the potency of the Hurricanes lineup was on display. In a game their top three point producers -- Sebastian Aho, Andrei Svechnikov and Jackson Blake -- were all held off the scoresheet, the Hurricanes converted both power-play opportunities with the depth players stepping forward. Ehlers and Jesperi Kotkaniemi scored their first goals of the season. Mark Jankowski extended his goal streak to six games, tying the franchise record since its relocation to Carolina from Hartford, Conn., for the 1997-98 season. Jankowski, who was drafted by the Flames in the first round in 2012 and set a career high with 17 goals in 2017-18 -- the first of his three full seasons in Calgary -- is trying to take his hot streak in stride. "It just feels great to help the team win any way possible," he said. "That's always been my philosophy. (I'm) just trying to do all the little things right and then eventually, the goals and all that come after." As the Flames are kicking off a four-game homestand, they sit at the bottom of the league standings. Calgary has managed only one win in seven outings, with all six defeats in regulation time. The team is back in action after suffering a 6-2 road loss to the Vegas Golden Knights on Thursday. The Flames fell behind on the game's first shot 25 seconds into the tilt and never recovered. "Take those puck-play mistakes or mishaps out of the equation, we did a lot of good things in the first period," coach Ryan Huska said. "But you're down 2-0 and against good teams, you can't give them leads like that where we're sitting." The Flames have dropped all three home games so far this season. The Vegas loss was even more deflating after Calgary had put together some solid performances, even in defeat, and was coming off its lone victory of the campaign, 4-2 at Anaheim on Tuesday. "We proved the two games prior we can play a really structured game," said defenseman Jake Middleton, who scored his first goal of the season in the loss. "We didn't (on Thursday) and it's something we can take as a lesson." Among the myriad reasons for Calgary's struggles is the sudden issue of penalties. The Flames were short-handed five times in each of the past two games, a trend in the first couple of outings that sent their season into a skid. "You take five or six penalties a night, you're not winning," Huska said. "There are quality players on the ice for too many minutes where they're able to touch the puck. It's not a good thing and it's not a recipe for success." --Field Level Media

item.title: Congo confirms Ebola outbreak has spread to eighth province
item.description: The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to an eighth province, North Ubangi, Congo's public health institute said on Sunday, confirming earlier Reuters reporting.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to an eighth province, North Ubangi, Congo's public health institute said on Sunday, confirming earlier Reuters reporting. The emergence of cases in the province, which borders Central African Republic, poses a new challenge for health authorities struggling to contain the outbreak. The National Institute for Biomedical Research confirmed two cases - including one death - in North Ubangi. Reuters [USN:L6N461199 TEXT:"reported on Thursday"] that two cases were confirmed in the province, citing two health officials. At the time, there was no official statement by Congolese authorities. North Ubangi becomes the eighth province affected by the outbreak, alongside North Kivu, Ituri, Haut-Uele, Tshopo, Sud-Kivu, Bas-Uele and South Ubangi. The outbreak, the worst Ebola epidemic in Congo's history, has already spread beyond the country's borders, with cases recorded in Uganda and seven infections [USN:L8N4621HW TEXT:"confirmed in Kenya"] this month. Congo's latest situation report showed 67 new confirmed cases and 26 new deaths in the 24 hours to Oct.16, bringing the cumulative total to 9,415 cases and 4,536 deaths since the outbreak began. The outbreak remains concentrated in eastern Congo, with Ituri province reporting 44 of the 67 new cases.

item.title: Blue Jackets try to build on success with road game vs. Wild
item.description: The Columbus Blue Jackets will seek their first winning streak of the young season on Sunday when they face the Minnesota Wild in Saint Paul, Minn.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The Columbus Blue Jackets will seek their first winning streak of the young season on Sunday when they face the Minnesota Wild in Saint Paul, Minn. Columbus needed overtime on Saturday before skating away with a 1-0 win over the visiting New York Rangers to stop a two-game skid. It was quite the turnaround from the Blue Jackets' previous game on Tuesday, when the visiting Florida Panthers rolled them 7-3. Defenseman Zach Werenski said after Saturday's win that it wasn't hard to hear the criticism about the team after the lopsided loss. However, the Blue Jackets, along with the Los Angeles Kings, have played the fewest games of any NHL team at six. "If you really look at the standings, everyone's kind of around the same spot right now, around .500," said Werenski, last season's Norris Trophy winner as the league's top defenseman. "We didn't want to fall behind that," he continued. "I think we're all aware of how we can play, how we have to play. Like I said, it wasn't perfect tonight but definitely a step in the right direction." Werenski picked up the primary assist on Kent Johnson's game-winning goal. Johnson leads the team with four goals, and Werenski's five assists are one behind Charlie Coyle's six. Coyle got the secondary helper to maintain the team lead. The Blue Jackets have scored just 17 goals in six games. However, Wild coach John Hynes said they're a physical team that can cause problems on the attack. "There's a lot of motion in the offensive zone, a lot of dives and rolls and things like that," Hynes said. "That always presents a challenge because you got to have the awareness to know where guys are going to be because they might not be in areas you think they're going to be." The Wild have two players who have combined for 14 goals in their eight contests. Kirill Kaprizov leads the NHL with nine goals this season, and Matt Boldy has five. Kaprizov also is tied for fifth with 14 points. Minnesota defenseman Quinn Hughes has 10 assists, tying him for fourth in the league. Minnesota has won three of four, beating the St. Louis Blues 5-4 on Thursday. Boldy had a hat trick in the game along with an assist. Kaprizov added a goal and two assists but left the game in the third period after taking a check from Blues goalie Joel Hofer. Kaprizov did not practice Saturday, but Hynes said it was because the forward was ill. Hynes' team has gotten off to a strong start this season despite a rash of injuries. That includes defenseman Jared Spurgeon, who has missed the last two games with an upper-body injury, and veteran Nick Foligno, who has been on injured reserve since Oct. 9 with an upper-body injury. Both practiced Saturday, but Hynes does not expect either to suit up Sunday. Jesper Wallstedt (5-1-1, 2.13 goals-against average, .920 save percentage) will start in goal for Minnesota for the eighth time this season. He faced the Blue Jackets for the first time last season, stopping 27 of 29 shots in a 5-2 win at Columbus on Dec. 18. With goaltender Jet Greaves getting the shutout Saturday, Columbus may turn to journeyman backup Cam Talbot (1-1, 4.43 GAA, .822 save percentage) on Sunday. In 21 career starts against the Wild, he owns a 9-9-3 record with a 2.64 GAA and .917 save percentage. --Field Level Media

item.title: Polish airports in Lublin, Rzeszow resume operations after temporary closure
item.description: Polish airports in the eastern city of Lublin and in Rzeszow, in the southeast, resumed flight operations following a temporary closure to allow for military aviation actions, the Polish Air Navigation Services Agency said in a post on X on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Polish airports in the eastern city of Lublin and in Rzeszow, in the southeast, resumed flight operations following a temporary closure to allow for military aviation actions, the Polish Air Navigation Services Agency said in a post on X on Sunday. Poland scrambled aircraft protectively to secure its airspace during Russia's strikes on neighbouring Ukraine. Earlier on Sunday Poland had said it was verifying a [USN:FWN4630JH TEXT:"possible violation of its airspace"] by an unidentified object.

item.title: Zelenskiy says Russia attacked Ukrainian energy sector 76 times in past week
item.description: Russia has attacked Ukraine's energy, oil and gas sectors dozens of times in the week since US President Donald Trump announced a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia has attacked Ukraine's energy, oil and gas sectors dozens of times in the week since US President Donald Trump announced a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Sunday. "Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ago, Russia has deliberately attacked Ukraine's energy and oil and gas sectors 76 times," he wrote on X, adding the latest strikes hit substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirmed Trump's announced ceasefire agreement.

item.title: Macron va s'adresser aux Français après les violences en marge des manifestations du 17 octobre
item.description: Emmanuel Macron s'adressera solennellement aux Français dimanche à 20h00, a annoncé l'Elysée au lendemain des scènes de violence et de pillages qui ont terni une journée de vaste mobilisation contre la vie chère dans toute la France.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Emmanuel Macron s'adressera solennellement aux Français dimanche à 20h00, a annoncé l'Elysée au lendemain des scènes de violence et de pillages qui ont terni une journée de vaste mobilisation contre la vie chère dans toute la France. Les maires de Paris, Lyon et Marseille, qui critiquent la gestion du maintien de l'ordre par l'exécutif, doivent être reçus à leur demande par le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu, qui a de son côté dénoncé une "violence d'une extrême intensité" organisée par des groupes d'ultragauche rejoints par des délinquants pour "piller et détruire". Des dégâts importants ont été rapportés dans de nombreuses grandes villes où des centaines de commerces ont été saccagés. La mairie de Limoges a été en grande partie détruite par un incendie. Initialement né sur les réseaux sociaux, l'appel à manifester le 17 octobre avait été relayé par les syndicats lycéens qui se mobilisent depuis la mi-septembre pour obtenir de meilleures conditions d'enseignement, ainsi que par des organisations syndicales. Le ministère de l'Intérieur a dénombré 550.000 manifestants dans tout le pays, dont 110.000 à Paris, la CGT faisant état pour sa part de 800.000 personnes dans les cortèges, qui se sont dans l'ensemble déroulés sans incident. PRINCIPAUX DÉVELOPPEMENTS : 14h30 - Le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, annonce sur X un nouveau bilan de plus de 2.000 personnes interpellées et de plus de 600 policiers, gendarmes et pompiers blessés. 12h55 - Dans un communiqué, la Confédération des commerçants de France, qui dit représenter plus de 7.000 TPE du commerce et de l'artisanat dans les centre-villes, estime que près de 1.500 commerces ont été touchés à travers la France samedi. 12h45 - Emmanuel Macron réunira à 17h30 à l'Elysée le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu et les ministres du gouvernement concernés et s'adressera solennellement aux Français à 20h00, annonce l'Elysée. 11h35 - "Je veux des explications et des moyens pour que cela ne se reproduise plus", déclare à la presse le maire socialiste de Marseille, Benoît Payan, alors que le ministre de l'Intérieur est attendu lundi dans la ville. "Mon propos n'est pas d'incriminer la police nationale. La police nationale, elle fait en fonction de qu'on lui demande (...). Je veux savoir quels ordres leurs ont été donnés, je veux savoir s'il leur a été demandé de s'occuper uniquement des manifestants et de lancer des lacrymos sur les manifestants et de ne pas s'occuper des pillages dans la ville." 11h20 - "Pendant une heure, je n'ai pas eu un seul policier national pour protéger la mairie", déclare sur BFM TV Guillaume Guérin, maire LR de Limoges. "On a un problème de soutien de nos forces de l'ordre", ajoute-t-il en déclarant avoir été informé par des policiers qu'ils manquaient de munitions. 11h00 - Le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, annonce sur X un bilan de 1.800 personnes interpellées samedi en France et de plus de 500 policiers, gendarmes et pompiers blessés. 10h45 - La secrétaire nationale des Ecologistes Marine Tondelier réclame sur X la démission du ministre de l'Intérieur Laurent Nuñez, "manifestement dépassé par la situation". 10h12 - "Ce bilan est désastreux car il emporte de lourdes conséquences : d’abord sur les libertés et notamment celle de manifester puisqu’elle est entravée par la violence ; ensuite sur la jeunesse confrontée à la brutalité et privée des réponses attendues du Gouvernement ; enfin sur l’État qui n’a pas été capable d’assurer partout l’ordre public", estime l'ancien président François Hollande dans un message sur X. 09h45 - A Lyon, le préfet du Rhône, Etienne Guyot, fait état de 160 personnes interpellées et placées en garde à vue et d'une centaine de membres des forces de l'ordre blessés. 08h50 - "Nous avons une ville dans une situation de délabrement total", déplore sur franceinfo la première adjointe au maire de Paris, Lamia El Araaje. "Nous avons assisté à des scènes de pillage méthodiques qui n'ont rien à voir avec les revendications sociales." "A l'évidence, les forces de l'ordre ont été débordées (...) Il y a eu clairement un manque de moyens", dit-elle. 08h15 - Une personne est décédée à la suite d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire samedi à Paris lors des manifestations contre la vie chère, pendant lesquelles 855 interpellations ont été effectuées, ce qui représente un "chiffre record", déclare la préfecture de police dans un bilan établi à 08h00. Treize policiers et gendarmes et deux sapeurs-pompiers ont été blessés, ajoute-t-elle.

item.title: Iran's parliament approves Mehrdad Akhlaqi as minister of defence
item.description: Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence minister on Sunday, ending months of interim leadership at the ministry and placing a former defence sector veteran in charge of the country's defence production and procurement apparatus.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence minister on Sunday, ending months of interim leadership at the ministry and placing a former defence sector veteran in charge of the country's defence production and procurement apparatus. Akhlaqi replaces Majid Ebn al-Reza, who took over in an interim capacity after then Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed by US-Israeli strikes in February. Akhlaqi has spent decades in Iran's defence industry and has held senior roles in its aerospace and missile sectors. He is subject to US and EU sanctions over his work in Iran's defence sector. In a programme presented to lawmakers, Akhlaqi pledged to rebuild the country's military-industrial infrastructure, accelerate the development of defence technologies and expand cooperation with private-sector companies. "If the American enemy makes another miscalculation, the response of the valiant Iranian people and the fighters of Islam will be surprising and extensive," he said, adding that Tehran had taken necessary measures to counter the potential use by the US of its "mother of all bombs" against Iran. CNN reported this week that the [USN:FWN46108H TEXT:"US has developed"] strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations. The weapon is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. "The US President should focus on ensuring his forces are withdrawn safely from our region. If he drops a single bomb, he will have to see how many of his troops end up being carried out of the region in a horizontal position," Akhlaqi said.

item.title: S Africa 11-0 after rain delays start of second test
item.description: South Africa were 11 for no wicket at lunch after rain curtailed play on the first day of the second test against Australia at St George’s Park on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: South Africa were 11 for no wicket at lunch after rain curtailed play on the first day of the second test against Australia at St George’s Park on Sunday. Aiden Markram was 10 not out and debutant Marques Ackerman on one as only 5.3 overs were possible in the first session. Rain delayed the start by two hours after Australia won the toss, with 27 minutes play before the covers came on again and lunch was taken early. Australia added an extra seamer to their attack with Scott Boland replacing Nathan Lyon. Kagiso Rabada returns to spearhead the home side’s pace attack after a lengthy injury in place of spinner Keshav Maharaj. South Africa dropped wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne with Ryan Rickelton taking the gloves and dropping down the batting ordert from opener to number six. Australia won the first test in Durban by 214 runs.

item.title: Rays, Guardians turn to All-Star pitchers in pivotal ALCS Game 5
item.description: CLEVELAND -- The American League Championship Series has become a best-of-three matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians splitting the first four games.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: CLEVELAND -- The American League Championship Series has become a best-of-three matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians splitting the first four games. Game 5 will be held Sunday in Cleveland, where Rays right-hander Drew Rasmussen (1-0, 1.29 ERA) takes on Guardians left-hander Parker Messick (0-2, 3.09) in a battle of 2026 All-Star selections.
